1.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh called]

Here, **in my ears** represents “in my hearing.” Yahweh is not directly addressing Ezekiel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my hearing] or [as I listened]
By **great**, here Yahweh means “loud.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with a loud voice]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **weapon** that is characterized by **destruction**. He means a weapon that is used for destroying people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with his weapon for destroying people]

1.q: קָרְב֖וּ פְּקֻדּ֣וֹת הָ⁠עִ֑יר וְ⁠אִ֛ישׁ כְּלִ֥י מַשְׁחֵת֖⁠וֹ בְּ⁠יָדֽ⁠וֹ
1.note: Here Yahweh addresses the **Executioners** in both second and third person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this using only the second person, as in the UST.

2.note: Here Ezekiel is introducing **Six men** and the man **clothed in linen**, as new participants in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And I saw that there were six men coming]

A **weapon of smashing** seems to be some kind of club used for killing animals or people. If your readers would not be familiar with what this is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with his heavy club]

The **equipment of the scribe** was a kind of case that held pens and ink and that a scribe wore at his waist. If your readers would not be familiar with what this equipment is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and a case for pens and ink]

3.note: If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar expression in 8:4. Alternate translation: [Then the glorious light indicating that the God of Israel was present]
The implication is that **the house** refers to the temple. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the threshold of the temple]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:2.

4.note: These phrases refer to the same place, not to two places. The second phrase gives the name of the city. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express these with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [through the midst of Jerusalem]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And you shall put a marking]

The word translated as **mark** is the name of the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which in Ezekiel’s time had the form of an “X.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And you shall draw a taw] or [And you shall make the mark of an X]

The terms **groaning** and **sighing** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the ones grieving deeply]

The expression **are being done** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that the people of Jerusalem were doing these things. Alternate translation: [that its inhabitants are committing]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:9.

5.note: Here, **in my ears** represents “in my hearing.” Yahweh is not directly addressing Ezekiel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my hearing] or [as I listened]

Here, **eye** represents the person as he looks at someone. The phrase **Do not let your eye pity** means “Do not feel pity when you look at these people.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. See how you translated the similar phrase, “My eye will not pity” in 8:18. Alternate translation: [Do not feel pity when you look at them]

6.note: Here, **Old man** and **young man** and **young woman** and **child** represent these kinds of people in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Old men, young men, young women, children]

The word translated as **young woman** usually refers to an unmarried woman, in contrast to the word translated as **women**, which would usually refer to married women. You could use a more specialized word in your translation if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [and maiden] or [and virgin]

Yahweh is using **do not draw near** as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not harm.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not touch him] or [do nothing]

7.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of his temple as a **house** and of making it unfit for worship as if it were becoming **unclean**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Make the temple ritually impure] or [Make my temple unfit for worship]

Yahweh is using the adjective **slain** as a noun to mean people who have been killed. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who have been killed]

8.note: The expression **I was left** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that I stayed there]

Falling face down on the ground was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed his distress and humility as he pleaded with Yahweh. He did not fall down accidentally. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And I lay face down on the ground in distress]
See how you translated this phrase in 4:14.

Ezekiel is speaking as if Yahweh’s **heat**, which represents his anger, were a liquid that he could **pour out**. It means that Yahweh is severely punishing the people because he is angry with them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you act so severely in your anger]

9.q: עֲוֺ֨ן בֵּֽית־יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל וִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ גָּדוֹל֙ בִּ⁠מְאֹ֣ד מְאֹ֔ד
9.note: If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The house of Israel and Judah has sinned very, very greatly]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Israel and Judah were a **house**, that is, a single household descended from one ancestor, Jacob. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Jacob in Israel and Judah]

Yahweh is repeating the word **very** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [extremely]
By **great** here, Yahweh means bad. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [bad] or [terrible]

The expression **is filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that the people of Israel and Judah did it. Alternate translation: [and they have filled the land with bloodshed]
Here, **bloodshed** represents “murder.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with violent killing]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **corruption**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people in this city constantly cheat each other]

9.q: אָמְר֗וּ עָזַ֤ב יְהוָה֙ אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠אֵ֥ין יְהוָ֖ה רֹאֶֽה
9.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [they say that Yahweh has abandoned the land and that Yahweh is not seeing]

10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:11 and 8:18.
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will not be compassionate]

Yahweh is using **Their way I have placed on their head** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will make them experience the consequences of the way that they have behaved.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will hold them accountable for their lifestyle] or [I will make them experience the consequences of the way that they have behaved]

11.note: Here, **a word** represents “a report.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [was bringing back a report]
